name: Coordinated Inauthentic Behavior
description: Detection and analysis of coordinated link-sharing and other inauthentic network behaviors on social media, including the CooRnet/CoorTweet methodology, workflow papers for monitoring coordinated accounts, and case studies from Italian, German, Nigerian and Ukrainian contexts. This is the researcher's signature methodological contribution and remains central to current publications and tools.

name: Generative AI and Media Manipulation
description: Study of how generative AI (LLMs, synthetic images/video, deepfakes, conversational agents) is used to produce persuasive, deceptive or manipulative content, and how it reshapes disinformation tactics and countermeasures. Reflected in recent publications on synthetic gambling promotion, LLM-based dashboards, and the new 'IA Generativa e Media' course.

name: Platform Governance and Research Data Access
description: Analysis of how platform policies, APIs, and regulatory frameworks (e.g., the Digital Services Act, Meta's URL Shares Dataset, CrowdTangle shutdown, political content reduction) shape what researchers and the public can see, and the methodological consequences for social media research.

name: Italian Political Communication (MINE Program)
description: The long-running Mapping Italian News (MINE) research line tracking Italian media and social media coverage of elections (2018, 2019, 2022), political parallelism, and campaign engagement — the institutional umbrella under which most of the researcher's empirical work is filed.

name: Computational Methods and LLM-Assisted Annotation
description: Development and validation of computational text-analysis pipelines, including embedding models for clustering political news and 'LLMs-in-the-loop' approaches for content classification and annotation in communication research, addressing challenges of reliability and disagreement.

name: Health Misinformation Networks
description: Mapping coordinated networks and gatekeeping dynamics that circulate problematic health information, including COVID-19 fact-checking acceleration and cross-national studies of health misinformation in India and Nigeria.

name: Political Polarization and Partisan Networks
description: Examination of partisan community dynamics, affective engagement, and polarization amplification across social and traditional media, including longitudinal studies of pro-Bolsonaro Facebook networks and comparative work on Latin American digital public debate.

name: News Diffusion and Platform Algorithms
description: Research on how algorithmic governance, partisan alignment and journalistic quality shape the circulation and visibility of news on social platforms, from cross-partisan interaction patterns to what 'millions see' on Facebook feeds.

name: Social TV and Second-Screen Engagement
description: Earlier but recurring strand analyzing audience participation, engagement and identity construction around television via Twitter and other second-screen social media use, foundational to the researcher's move into large-scale social media data analysis.

name: Sociocybernetics and Social Systems Theory
description: Theoretical work bridging sociocybernetics and internet studies, exploring social systems theory as a lens for understanding networked communication — a foundational, lower-frequency but persistent thread underlying the researcher's broader empirical agenda.

name: Platforms, Audiences, and Online Communities
description: Empirical and reflective studies of how platform affordances, cultures, and audience practices shape online sociality, identity, and community formation across sites like Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, Twitter/Mastodon, and LiveJournal.

name: Critical Analysis of AI Industry Imaginaries and Discourse
description: Studies examining how AI industry actors, media, and communities construct and circulate narratives, imaginaries, and framings (e.g., longtermism, techno-hagiography, 'quiet futuring', political-economy 'decoys') that shape public understanding and obscure or legitimize the underlying power structures of AI development.

name: Reflections on the State of Misinformation and Online Harm Research
description: Papers that step back from primary empirical study to critically assess the misinformation/online-harms research field itself — diagnosing biases (e.g., WEIRD-centrism, overreliance on cognitive proxies), mapping gaps in evidence (causal, longitudinal, cross-national), and proposing directions or borrowed lessons (e.g., from climate psychology) to make the field more rigorous and generalizable.
